messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Not practicing. Avoiding, maybe. I’ve been feeling off about how I handled something, and I don’t want this to come out wrong.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: That sounds a lot like the start of a speech people give when they want room to back out of every word. If this is about us, just say it.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: I kissed Mara at Theo's party, and I've been trying to tell you before someone else did. It was two weeks ago.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Mara. Your Mara Mara. And this whole drive, I’m over here thinking you’re about to talk about some vague distance thing while you’ve been carrying that around?

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: I wasn’t trying to make you guess wrong. I should’ve said it the second I started talking. I just kept hearing it one way in my head and none of it sounded less bad.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You were trying to tell me before someone else did. That part landed very clearly. So who knows?

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Theo saw, and maybe Sam did. Nobody said anything to you, at least not yet. I didn’t want you hearing some party version first.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Not yet is doing a lot of work there. Two weeks of dinners, your goodnight calls, you asking if I wanted to go see your sister on Sunday. You found room for all of that.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: I know how that looks. I kept thinking there was a better moment than when you were slammed at work, or when your mom was in town, or right before bed. Then it just got uglier every day I waited.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Was it one of those things where everyone was drunk and nostalgic and somehow that’s supposed to blur the edges? Or was this a long conversation first, catching up, the whole old-song soundtrack version?

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: We talked, yeah. Then it happened, and I pulled back right after. I left early, and I haven’t seen her since.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You keep giving me the shortest possible answers like that helps. It doesn’t. Right now the kiss is one thing, and the version of you sitting next to me for fourteen days is another.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Then ask whatever you want and I’ll answer it straight. I’m not going to trim it down or make it prettier now. You shouldn’t have had to pull it out of me in a car.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Can we not do this right here by the window? Half the floor can hear a chair move in this corner. Just come a little farther back between the stacks.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: No, we're not disappearing between shelves so you can twist this around on me. I'm not going to stand here and be painted as the bad one again. If you came over to accuse me, say it where people can hear every word.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Keep your voice down. I'm not putting on a show in a library, Kendall. This needs to be handled without four freshmen pretending not to stare at us over their flashcards.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: There it is. You walk up, tell me to lower my voice, and act like I'm the one making a scene. Maybe start with why you're here instead of trying to manage me.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I'm here because this got bigger than people whispering after class. And every time I try to get one sentence out, you decide volume means you're right. Please, not here.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Bigger than whispers because somebody kept repeating a version that wasn't what I said. I've already had enough people looking at me like I started something on purpose. I'm not helping you pin the whole thing on me.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You really think I came over with an audience in mind? Look around. I keep asking you to step aside because this is already ugly enough without turning the study tables into a jury box.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Then stop circling and say what you came to say. You don't get to lean in and talk like that and expect me to follow you somewhere quieter so I can be cornered into agreeing with whatever version helps you.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: That is not what this is. You hear one request to not broadcast across the reference section and suddenly it's some trap. I'm trying to keep both of us from ending up as entertainment.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Funny, because from where I'm standing, you came straight over here ready to decide what this looks like before I even opened my laptop. If you want something from me, stop acting like I should already know what game you're playing.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Fine. This is not me trying to corner you. A staff member contacted me this morning because there is already a complaint, and your name came up as someone who can clear it up. If we stop arguing and compare what each of us actually knows, we can handle this before it gets worse.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: What exactly was said? Start from the beginning, and don't skip over the part where my name came up. Who contacted you?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Someone in the department office called after nine. They said there'd been a report about comments going around and asked whether I wanted to add anything formally. Then they said your name had been mentioned as someone who might know how the story got distorted.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Distorted is the right word. I said one thing to Mira after seminar, and by the next day it came back sounding like I'd announced it to the whole building. I stayed out of it because every time my name gets attached to drama, somehow I end up carrying all of it.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Mira. No one gave me that name before. What reached me sounded polished, like it had passed through three people already, which is why the office calling felt so surreal.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: I never said it the way people repeated it. She asked why you dropped the committee thing, and I said there had been tension with the supervisor and you were tired of being discussed like a project. That somehow turned into something much uglier.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: The version I heard had you telling people I was unstable and impossible to work with. That's what the complaint is orbiting around. If the office asks again, can you say where your part ended and where hers started?

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Yes, but I'm not signing up to be the lone villain and then the cleanup crew. If they want a statement, I'll give one with dates and who was there. And I'm not doing it as some vague apology for words I didn't use.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: That's fair. I can forward the email and the number they left, and we can make sure the timeline matches before either of us replies. Better that than letting whoever embellished it keep hiding behind 'everyone was saying it.'

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Send it. I'll write out exactly what I said to Mira and when, and you can add what the office told you. Then if anyone asks in person, we stick to that instead of doing this in front of the biography section again.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Hi, Riley. Thanks for joining—I've already got the packet up on share, and the due line is here at the top in red. Can you send the source file for Appendix C, or approve us to use the version we were sent, by end of day?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Morning. Before I answer that, I want to make sure we're talking about the same file. Is this the internal worksheet behind Appendix C, or the formatted export that's already in your packet?

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: The internal worksheet, the one with the final numbers and tabs intact. The team assembling this needs the underlying file, and if that's not possible today, then a clear approval to proceed with the version we have would cover us.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: All right. I prefer to be precise about those two options because they aren't the same on our side. The worksheet and any release decision sit in a controlled lane.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Understood, and I'm not trying to blur them. I just need to leave this call knowing whether the package can be completed today, because the rest of it is ready and this is the piece holding the line.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I heard the timing. What I'm trying to establish is why my approval is the one being asked for here. Usually requests like this come through with the release path already identified.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Your name was the one attached to the latest revision notes, so that's where I started. If there's another stop after you, I can work with that, but I do need something firmer than 'maybe later' before this afternoon.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I haven't said 'maybe later.' I've said I need to be accurate before I confirm anything. Those are different.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Fair enough. Then let me put it plainly: if the request lands correctly, does this move today, or should I stop telling people to expect it?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I need to be clear: I cannot authorize that myself. The file is under my team's controls, and I have to get my lead's written sign-off before anything is released.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: All right, that changes the map. I took your name on the revision notes to mean the handoff could happen directly through you. What does your lead need to see to make that decision?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: A written request with the purpose, the exact file name, who will receive it, and whether the workbook stays internal or gets redistributed. If you send that to me and copy the department lead, I can attach the current record and move it along quickly.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I can do that within the hour. If the workbook itself doesn't clear, would a written note from your lead on the formatted export still let the packet go out cleanly?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Yes, if the note specifies that the export is the approved artifact for external use. That's simpler than releasing the worksheet, and it's more likely to get a same-day answer.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That helps. I'll revise the ask so it points to the export first, and I'll send the fuller request right after this call. If there's a preferred subject line or reference code, include that and I'll use it exactly.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Use the project code from the footer on your shared document and mark it as a release request. Once it comes through, I'll add the internal tracking note and forward it to my lead. That should keep it moving without anyone guessing.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Your aunt said to leave this here, but I remember your mother always moved casseroles away from the stove. Some things in this kitchen never change. You still come in through the side hall when you want a second before facing everybody.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I know how this must have looked. Earlier, I mean, and probably before that too. I didn't want you walking into this house with everything still twisted.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Twisted for who. Because in the dining room it sounded like everyone had already settled on a version that works fine for them. You got very precise very fast.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I'm trying not to make this worse five minutes before dinner. A lot of what happened came across harsher than it was. That doesn't mean it was nothing.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Do you really think that's what this was about? Things coming across badly. Because that's a neat way to package a lot of mess.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: If you want me to say I handled it badly, I did. I should have explained more instead of disappearing behind reasons that sounded convenient. I'm not pretending that landed lightly.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You're still answering a charge I didn't make. And you keep looking at that doorway like someone's about to grade us. I'm standing right here.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Because this isn't exactly private, Ellis. And because when you bring up what was said in there, I assume you're not bringing it up casually. I thought you were asking me to finally say the obvious part out loud.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: The obvious part to who. Your cousins who think every silence needs a villain. Or you, because you've already written my side so thoroughly you don't need to hear it.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Then tell me where I'm wrong. Because I walked in here expecting you had every reason to see me exactly the way they do. I figured if we were doing this, that was the ground we were standing on.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That's the part that keeps landing wrong. You talk like I've been carrying their script around and waiting for my turn to read it back to you. Last month I had to listen to them talk about you like you were some calculated disaster.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I heard there was an argument. I didn't know what you said, only that your name came up and then everything got quiet when I entered the room today. So yes, I filled in the blanks.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You filled them in with the worst one. I wasn't defending myself with your family, Riley. I was defending you.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You were. After all this time. I thought you agreed with them, or at least had no reason not to, and I've been talking to you like I needed to win back a verdict.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That was the part I couldn't seem to get past. You came in smoothing every edge before I even said anything, like my place in this was just another accusation to manage. It wasn't small, standing there and not joining in.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I know. And I made you carry that alone, then met you here like you were about to hand me a sentence. Thank you for not letting them turn me into something simpler than I was, and I'm sorry I assumed you already had.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I didn't need a perfect speech. Just not that look people get when they've decided I'm only bringing up old wreckage for effect. Hearing you say it plainly helps.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Then let me say one plain thing before we go back in. I should have trusted that you knew me better than that. If you can stand beside me in there after everything, I can stop talking like I'm on trial.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: So you just went ahead and did it. New job, new place, all tied up before this call. Nice to hear about a decision for both of us after the paperwork's already done.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: That's not what this was about. And your camera is tilted, by the way; I can barely see half your face. This was my move, not some joint file you got left out of.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Right, there it is, the wording. 'My move,' like that changes what it touched. You didn't get to decide alone and then call it neat because you picked the right label.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I'm not picking labels. I'm being specific because you're making it sound like I rearranged your life from my desk. I accepted a position and handled the housing attached to it.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Handled the housing attached to it, sure. You always sound very reasonable when you're locking something in before anyone else can say a word. Then suddenly the only problem is tone.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: No, the problem is scope. You opened with 'both of us' like that was still an active category for where I live and what contract I sign. It wasn't.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Funny how that category disappears exactly when it's useful to you. You knew this wasn't some tiny update. You knew it changed things, and you kept moving like there was nothing to discuss.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Changed things compared to what, Marlowe? You keep talking as if there was a seat at the table I pulled away at the last second. There wasn't a table.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Don't do that. Don't act like this is me being dramatic because I noticed you crossed another line and decided it didn't count. You don't get to erase the practical part just because the rest went bad.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I signed the lease because the move is only for me; there was never a 'we' attached to it, and hearing you call it our decision makes it sound like you still think you were part of that plan. That's the piece you've been building this on. There wasn't anything for me to clear with you.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I didn't realize that's where you had it set. You could've said that before the contract language lecture. I was talking like there was still shared ground there.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I tried to say it at the start, just less bluntly. You came in like this was another round of me making some statement at you. It wasn't a statement; it was logistics.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Fine. Logistics. Then I was arguing over a blueprint that wasn't on the table anymore.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yes. And I didn't want to spell it out that hard on a screen like this, but apparently softer versions leave room for fiction. The move is mine, the lease is mine, and that's all it was.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Got it. Congratulations on the job, then. I don't have much else to add.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Thank you. I hope things on your side settle out cleanly too. We can end here.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I got here early, so I guessed on your order. If this is the wrong kind, I can trade. Also, I moved the laptop out of the way so it stops pretending to be invited.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: You guessed right, which is either impressive or a little alarming. And the corner table was a good call; the rest of the place sounds like an espresso machine arguing with itself.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: That machine has been doing that for ten minutes. I was timing it instead of opening the article for seminar, which probably explains why my notes are still bad.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Your notes are never bad. Half the time I'm still decoding the prompt and you've already found the one sentence everyone else missed.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: You say that, and then somehow your comments are the ones the professor writes down. It's a suspicious system. I may need to file a complaint.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Please do, but make it flattering. Also, thanks for the coffee. This feels nicer than our usual library table with the broken chair.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: The broken chair builds character. This is better, though. Less fluorescent lighting, fewer undergrads conducting their entire emotional lives three feet away.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: That's true. It's easier to hear yourself think in here. Or at least easier to say things without the library making them sound illegal.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: That sounds like a setup line. Should I be worried, or just finish my coffee first?

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Finish your coffee if you want, but it's not that dramatic. I was just going to ask something that isn't about the midterm or office hours for once.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: That narrows it down to several thousand possibilities. Go ahead.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Do you want to hang out sometime when it's not about class? Like, on purpose, not because one of us has a question or a deadline.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I do. I... there is one thing, though. I got offered a summer research placement in Madison, and there's a pretty strong chance I'll be there most of the summer.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Oh. Okay, that explains the pause a lot better than the version I was writing in my head. Madison is a big thing.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I should have mentioned it earlier. It came through this week, and every time there was a normal moment to bring it up, it stopped being a normal moment.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: You don't need to apologize for getting offered something good. I just wasn't asking with a spreadsheet open. So the silence landed a little differently before the actual reason showed up.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Right. I realized that about halfway through being silent, which was not ideal. For the record, this wasn't me looking for a neat exit.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: That's good to know. I wasn't aiming for a five-year plan, either. I just didn't want to keep pretending coffee only counts if there's a reading attached.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Then yes, still yes. We could do something before I leave, and after that we can see what survives bad schedules and geography. That sounds less elegant out loud, but it feels more honest.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Honest works. We can start with something simple and local while you've still got this corner table jurisdiction. Then if Madison steals you for a while, at least this won't have stayed in the library forever.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Hey. This corner's a little quieter than the middle, if that helps. I was about to sit down.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Yeah, it's so loud in here today. Every tray sounds like it's hitting the floor. Are you still eating here, or— can I take that seat?

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: You can. I haven't started yet. The line took forever anyway.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: I figured. The sandwich station looked impossible when I walked in. Your pasta actually looks better than what I got.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: It's probably fine once it cools down. Cafeteria food has low standards to meet. Yours looks like it survived a small war.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: That's fair. I should've aimed lower. Um, did you just get here?

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Not just now. Long enough to finish half a water and watch three people steal forks from the napkin stand. It was kind of impressive.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Oh. Right. I came over as soon as I got in here. I wasn't sure if you'd already left.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I thought about it. Then I figured I'd at least eat first. No reason to waste decent pasta on timing.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Okay. Thanks for staying, I guess. You seem... I don't know, a little off.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Do I? You seemed busy. Or maybe just hard to reach. Either way, lunch kept moving without much input from me.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: It wasn't really like that. I mean, I know this got weird. I was trying to figure out how to say it without making it worse.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: You could've started with that instead of reviewing the acoustics and my pasta. When somebody sends a time and gets nothing back, it sort of narrows the possibilities.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: I know. That's why I came over. You looked like you wanted this to be quick, so I wasn't sure how to jump in.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: If you didn't want to have lunch with me, you could've just said that.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: I didn't ignore you; my phone died in class, and I only saw your text right before I came over. That's why I paused over there for a second—I saw the message and then saw you standing here looking like you were about to leave.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Oh. That makes a lot more sense than what I put together from across the room. I probably made this sharper than it needed to be.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: It's okay. I should've led with that instead of talking about trays and pasta like an idiot. Can we start over while your lunch is still warm?

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Move, I'm going back to room 214. The bell already rang, and you're blocking the whole corridor. Give me that for one second.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Not one second. Mr. Bennett handed me this and said it came from under your desk, and then he sent me here before you disappeared again. You're not rushing past the principal's office like nothing happened.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: I wasn't disappearing, I was turning around. I picked it up after class because somebody dropped it, and if you'd stop standing in front of me, I could put it back where it belongs. People are staring.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Don't start making excuses. You've been pointing at that classroom since I called your name, like saying 'it's back there' fixes anything. Tell me why this was under your desk.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Because it slid there when Liam knocked his stuff off the table, okay? He left fast, I saw this on the floor, and I grabbed it. I was trying to get it back before Mr. Bennett saw me holding it and did exactly this.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Then you could have said that without trying to keep walking away. Every time I ask a straight question, you hitch that bag up and angle down the hall. That makes this look worse, not better.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Because you came at me with a crumpled note outside the principal's door like the verdict was already done. You didn't even let me finish one sentence before 'don't start' came out. So yeah, I was trying to get back there first.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: I let you finish when I get something solid. Right now I've got your teacher saying one thing and you saying 'trust me' while half the seventh grade slows down to watch. I'm asking once more: what's in it and whose is it?

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: I didn't open it. I know whose handwriting it isn't, if that helps. The front got crumpled, but the name's inside if you'd actually unfold it instead of waving it at me.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: You're suddenly very sure for someone who says they never read it. Why wouldn't you just hand it to the teacher instead of pocketing it and sprinting off? That part still doesn't add up.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Because once it's in a teacher's hand and it's near my desk, guess who gets attached to it. Read the name inside if you don't believe me. It's there, on the fold.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: ...Fine. This says Nora Patel. All right—fine, we go back to the classroom together and ask Mr. Bennett before anyone goes in there.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Good. Nora was two rows over by the windows, and Liam was messing around near her table when his binder hit the floor. Ask him too, since apparently everything needs three witnesses.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: We'll ask whoever was there. Keep your voice down and walk with me. If Mr. Bennett mixed up where he found it, we'll sort that out there instead of out here.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: I'm walking with you. And when we get there, let me talk before you hold the paper up like it's Exhibit A again. Nora folds all her notes like that anyway.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Then point her out and say exactly what you saw. I'll hand this back to Mr. Bennett and we'll clear up who dropped what. Come on, before they lock the classroom.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Hey. You've been parked by these lockers for, what, two minutes just staring at the dent in mine. Can you just tell me what's going on?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Nothing. You're going to be late if you keep stopping in the middle of the hallway.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Don't do the one-word thing with me. If I missed something, say it before the bell traps us on opposite sides of the building.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: If you don't get it, that's kind of the problem. You've been acting like this stuff doesn't matter.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: What stuff? I texted you back last night, and I saved you a seat in chem, so if this is about me being flaky lately, just say that.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Right, because this is definitely about chem. Forget it.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I'm not trying to drag this out, Hayden. I seriously don't know what this is about, and you're looking at the clock like you're going to make me guess until class starts.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Maybe guessing would help. Since apparently saying things directly is hard today.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Okay, was it lunch? Did I say something dumb by the vending machines? Or are you still mad I forgot your notebook on Friday, because that at least would make sense.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You keep doing that. Listing random things like one of them will cover it.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Because you're giving me absolutely nothing back. I walked over here to fix whatever this is, not stand here getting iced out in front of half the sophomore class.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: I saw you by the stairs laughing with Maya like I wasn't even there. Then you come over here acting like this came out of nowhere.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I was asking her about your birthday surprise, not flirting. That's why I was being weird this week, because she was helping me not ruin it.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Oh. That... looks different from across the hallway when you don't know any of that.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: You could've just said Maya's name before making me speedrun every mistake I've made since Friday. And for the record, if it had been anything else, I still would've stopped.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Yeah, okay. I should've just asked instead of standing here like a statue. Are we good, or do I owe you one dramatic apology and half my fries at lunch?

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Look at this paragraph on the screen. If we build from this example first, half the introduction basically writes itself. Also, your note piles are starting to look like a library checkout desk.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: The checkout desk is keeping us from losing things under your coffee-stained printouts. Can we decide the order before we chase examples? We have books open everywhere already.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: We can figure the order out once we get into it. The article is the whole point, and if we stop to label every step first, we'll drain the life out of it.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I'm not labeling every step. I'm asking what comes first, what supports it, and who handles which part. That's not exactly a bureaucratic nightmare.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: You just slid the article aside without even opening the tab I marked. That usually means the interesting part has been demoted to 'later,' which somehow becomes never.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I moved it so I could clear a space to write. If we don't have an outline and a task split, we'll end up with three great fragments and no paper.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Or we'll end up with one clean outline and nothing worth putting under the headings. This example gives us a center, and you keep steering back to boxes and numbers.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Because boxes and numbers are how things get finished on time. Every time I ask about division of work, you point back to the laptop like the rest will sort itself out.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Maybe because the laptop has the argument on it. Opening a fresh page called 'Plan' before we've even talked through the best angle makes it look like the angle has already been decided somewhere without me.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: That's not fair. I haven't decided the angle; I've asked about the order three times because I'd rather not guess who is doing what at midnight tomorrow.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: And I'd rather not watch the strongest idea get parked while we build a frame around an empty wall. When you go all clipped and practical like this, it sounds like you've already stamped my stuff 'optional.'

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I am not trying to box you in; I am asking for a basic outline because I want us to work well together. Your example can lead, but I need some shape around it so we're not tripping over each other.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Oh, I thought you were shutting my ideas down, not trying to make this easier for both of us. That's different from how it was landing from across the table.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Across the table probably looks harsher when I'm sorting paper into little piles. I wasn't putting your article in exile. I just didn't want us drifting into separate projects under the same title.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Okay, that makes more sense than the tiny paper exile. I kept dragging us back to the screen because I didn't want the main point buried under setup. If the outline stays basic, I can work with that.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Basic I can do. We start with your article as the anchor, sketch three sections, and split the sources after that. Then if you find another angle while we're writing, it has somewhere to go.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Three sections is fine. Put the example first, then the broader argument, then the comparison source from that blue book. I can pull quotes while you set up the skeleton.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Deal. And once I stop guarding the note piles like a suspicious archivist, you can show me the tab you kept trying to get me to open. I assume that's the part you've been waving at for ten minutes.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Yes, and it's worth the ten-minute campaign. The second paragraph links almost perfectly with that reference book by your elbow, so your neat stacks may actually get their moment.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Good, then the stacks and the screen can call a truce. Open the tab, and I'll write the section headings while you tell me where that paragraph fits.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: This place is louder by the bar than it looked from the door. I had to fight two elbows just to get these drinks over here. Thanks for grabbing that spot before someone slid into it.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You got back in one piece, so that's a win. The counter's sticky, but it's prime people-watching. What's with the undercover voice all of a sudden?

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Nothing dramatic. I just didn't want to yell it over whatever remix this is. You know that new bar project your friend is tied to?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Depends which one. Lately everybody's either opening a bar or talking about opening a bar. Why?

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: The one downtown, near the old record shop. I heard they're still staffing up, and it's honestly not a big thing. I just wanted to ask you something without making it weird.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Saying it's not weird usually means it's about to be at least a little weird. Go on.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Okay. I was hoping you could put in a word for me with your friend on that new bar project. Just so my name doesn't land in the pile with everybody else's.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I don't do friend-to-friend referrals like that anymore. If somebody wants staff, they can hire off experience and interviews, not because they know me.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Right. Fast answer. I wasn't trying to wedge myself in through your contacts like that.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You asked me to put in a word. That's exactly what that is. I keep that stuff separate now.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: I said it badly. I wouldn't ask if I had another easy option, and I wasn't looking for some VIP side door. I just need work that starts soon, that's all.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Soon as in this week soon? Because that sounds different from just wanting a better gig. Still doesn't change the referral part.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Soon as in my landlord stopped using smiley faces. My cousin's opening a place too, but that one won't start paying for another month, and I'm trying not to do the whole family rescue circuit. So I asked you.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Okay. That's rough, and I'm not brushing it off. But when people start tying money to friendship, it gets ugly fast, and I'm not stepping into that lane again.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: You could've said that before the ice-water answer. For a second it sounded like you had me sorted before I finished the sentence. That's a fun feeling to have while holding a margarita.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Fair. I clocked the setup too early and came in hard. I won't call my friend, but I'll look at your resume tonight, and if that place has a public posting, I'll help you make it sharper than the pile.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: That helps more than pretending you never heard me. I can live with a straight line, even if it's got barbed wire on it. I'll send it over after I fix the part where I made 'hosting brunch' sound like military service.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Good, because if your resume says you survived bottomless mimosas, that's basically combat-tested. Send it before midnight and I'll take a swing at it. Next round stays on you, though.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You just put it face down right after showing me half a line. Between the trays rattling and everyone yelling over each other, I'm already having to guess what you mean. Who sent that?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Can you not make it sound dramatic in the middle of the cafeteria? It's not a big deal. I only showed you because it popped up while we were talking.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Then say what it is. You showed me enough to make it look important, then stopped right before the part that mattered. That's a weird thing to do if there's nothing there.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: It's family stuff, okay? I don't want to unpack it next to the soda machine while somebody from your office is two tables over. Can we just eat?

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Family stuff is not an answer. Who exactly sent that, and why won't you just say it? You keep clipping everything down to one vague sentence.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Because every time I pause for one second, you turn into a prosecutor. I said it was family. That should count for something.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: No, what counts is context. This week it's been your phone buzzing, then plans getting moved, then this. You don't get to hand me a puzzle piece and act surprised when I ask where the rest is.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Wow, okay, so that's what this is about. You could have said that instead of circling me over a message. I canceled one night, Shiloh, not my entire life with you.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I'm asking because you keep making me drag basic information out of you. 'It's not a big deal,' 'family stuff,' 'not here'—what am I supposed to do with that? Sit here and pretend that sounds normal?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Maybe trust that not everything awkward is some secret double life. Maybe don't lean across the table like you're waiting for me to slip up. This is exactly why I didn't want to get into it here.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Wait, this is from your sister asking for money? I thought you were hiding who it was. The preview says car repair.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Yes. She needed help fast, and I didn't want to announce that across a room full of people while balancing fries and a drink. That's all it was.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I didn't see that part at first. I saw you flip the phone over and shut everything down, and I filled in the blanks badly. I'm sorry.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I could've just said it instead of hiding behind 'family stuff.' It's just embarrassing when this keeps happening, and I hate making it sound like chaos follows me around. But it wasn't what you were thinking.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I know that now. And for the record, the canceled night and all the texting had me reading every little thing too hard. I should've asked like a person, not cross-examined you over mashed potatoes.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: The mashed potatoes did not deserve that energy. Neither did you, honestly. Next time I'll just say, 'my sister is in a mess again,' and we can save the courtroom scene for somewhere with less fluorescent lighting.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Deal. Is she stranded, or is it one of those repair shops that says 'urgent' and then starts adding things? You don't have to do the whole thing alone just because it's annoying.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Her car died on the way to work, and the estimate is ugly enough that she panicked before I even finished my sandwich. I can show you the whole message this time. Then maybe we can eat something before it goes completely cold.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Your coffee's getting cold. Want mine instead? I barely touched it.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: No, keep it. Reese, can you look at me for a second instead of your cup lid or whatever's in your hands? Things have felt off lately.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: I'm looking at you now. It's just getting dark, that's all. What feels off?

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: You tell me. You're here, but not really here, and every time I ask how your day went, I get three words and a shrug. That's not nothing.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Work's been busy. Not every quiet week means a disaster. You make it sound bigger than it is.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Then make it smaller by actually saying something real. I shouldn't have to drag basic honesty out of you on a park bench after pretending to enjoy takeout coffee.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: You want honesty? Fine. You're acting like I skipped town without telling you. I've just had a lot on my plate.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: That's exactly the kind of answer I'm talking about. "A lot on my plate" could mean anything, and somehow I'm supposed to smile and let it go. I'm not doing that tonight.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: So what, you want a speech? You want me to say everything's okay so we can go home and call it handled? Because that's usually where this lands.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: No, actually, that's the part you seem determined not to hear. I'm asking whether this is still something you're in, or whether you've been slowly backing away and hoping I won't say it first.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: That's a pretty dramatic version of this. I've still shown up, haven't I? Sitting here counts for something.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Showing up and disappearing while you're sitting next to me are two different things. You keep checking whatever that is in your hand like it's easier to deal with than me. So tell me what I'm supposed to do with that.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Maybe not turn every pause into a verdict. Maybe let a conversation breathe for five seconds without deciding how it ends. Not everything is a code.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Funny, because this feels exactly like a code, and I'm the only one expected to solve it. You don't get to go silent and then blame me for noticing. If you need distance, say distance.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: You keep pushing this toward some final sentence. Maybe I'm waiting to hear something from you that isn't just a complaint about my tone.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: If you already have one foot out the door, just say it.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: I got offered a job in Portland last week, and I needed to know whether us mattered enough for you to actually say so. You kept circling around feeling shut out, but you never said what you'd do if something real changed.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: You sat on that for a week and turned this into some kind of trial? Portland isn't a bad mood or a long day, Reese. You don't get to dangle a whole other city in front of us and wait to see if I perform correctly.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: I know how it looks. Every time things get serious, you ask for comfort first and the bigger question gets parked, so I waited. That was cheap, and now it's out—so what happens if it's not just tonight and not just this bench?

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Then ask me straight next time. Don't make me guess whether I'm losing you while you're secretly comparing zip codes. I'm here, and I'm not casual about you, but I won't keep doing this if important things come wrapped in tests.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: You always pick the quiet corner when the lunch crowd thins out. Your coffee's getting cold. I wasn't sure if this was about the schedule or... something else.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: It's easier to talk here without everyone walking past. And the schedule does need sorting out. How's your morning been?

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Full of people asking for updates like I keep the master map in my pocket. I was going to ask you something, actually. It's probably better if I don't phrase it badly.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: All right. Ask it. There's something I need to explain too, so maybe we're circling the same thing.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: That sounds promising. Or not promising, depending on the version. Have you heard anything odd from upstairs lately?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: People upstairs are always saying odd things. I wouldn't put much weight on hallway chatter. If there's a specific issue, just say the specific issue.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Right. Specific would help. It's just that when people start mentioning coverage and continuity, it can sound like a decision got made before anyone in the room was told.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You're not wrong about that. Things do get discussed before they land where they should. I didn't want this to come across like I was dropping it on your tray between bites.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: So there is a 'this.' Okay. If this is about responsibilities shifting around, I'd rather hear it straight than piece it together from half-sentences.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I know. That's fair. I kept putting the words in the wrong order.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I've been doing the same thing, apparently. Every version in my head sounds worse out loud. Go ahead.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I should just say it—I accepted a transfer out of the team. Next month, I'm moving to the operations group.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Then I need to tell you they asked me to take over some of your work, and I did not ask for that. It came through my manager two days ago, and I kept trying to figure out whether you already knew.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I didn't know they'd already brought your name into it. That explains a lot, actually. We probably could've skipped ten minutes if we'd both started with the first sentence.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Probably, yes. I heard myself talking like I was smuggling contraband in a paper cup. If they're serious about shifting things over, I'd rather go through it with you directly than let everyone else improvise.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: That's better than letting rumor do the handoff. I'll map out the coordination pieces and the deadlines, and you can tell me what doesn't make sense. Next time, we skip the cautious small talk and lead with the part that matters.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: You found the one stool with the sticky ring on it. Lucky you. The bartender's been polishing that same glass for ten minutes, so I guess we're both early for something.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Yeah. Can we just clear up what happened that night? You've been weird with me ever since.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: That's one way to open. And no, it wasn't just that night. It kind of kept going after that.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Okay, then tell me which part. The canceled plan, not texting after, whatever else—just say it straight so I know what I'm answering.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: You make it sound like a customer service form. Pick a box, circle the issue, move on. That's not really the part that lands the hardest.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: I'm not trying to do that. I'm trying not to guess wrong again. You stopped talking to me like two words at a time, so yeah, I'm asking.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: You didn't seem too worried when it first happened. People vanish all the time in places like this, then show up a week later and act like nothing bent. It's hard to tell what's supposed to matter.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: I didn't vanish for fun. I missed one plan, and after that every time I saw you, it felt like you were waiting for me to say the wrong thing. So what exactly did you want from me?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Not a perfect speech. Not a bullet-point defense. Just something that sounded like I existed in the story, maybe.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: You did. That's why I'm here now instead of pretending it's fine. But if this is about me ditching you on purpose, that's not what happened.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: I already heard why you left that night—your brother had a car accident. What hurt was that everyone else seemed to know before I did, and you never told me yourself.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Wait—you knew that already? I didn't know anyone had told you. I should've called you myself, and I didn't.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Hearing it from somebody else at a coffee shop was... not great. It made the whole thing feel like I was close enough to get canceled on, but not close enough for the actual reason. That's the part that stuck.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: That's fair. I was at the hospital, then with him, then sleeping in scraps, and I handled the rest badly. You shouldn't have had to piece it together from other people.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: I wasn't asking for a dramatic update from the waiting room. Just one message with my name in it would have changed the whole shape of it. Instead it sat there and got uglier the longer it went.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: You're right. I'm sorry I left you to fill in the blanks, and I'm sorry I came in tonight like this was a schedule problem. Next time something blows up, you'll hear it from me, not the neighborhood grapevine.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: This pond always makes everything slow down. Even the ducks look like they have nowhere to be. Do you want to sit for a minute, or keep walking with those very ambitious coffees?

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: We can stop. Mine's still too hot anyway. That bench is empty, which feels like a minor miracle this time of day.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You always notice the useful part first. I notice the light on the water and you notice available seating. Have you ever thought about us differently, or is that a strange question for a bench by a pond?

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: It's not strange. Just... complicated. And this week has been a lot.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Okay. You don't have to answer if it's weird. I just kept catching myself wondering whether the extra dinners and the late-night kitchen talks were only our usual thing with better snacks.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Those weren't nothing. I wouldn't call them routine. We do need to figure out groceries for next week, though, because we're somehow out of everything except mustard and frozen peas.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Right, groceries. That's usually where difficult conversations go to disappear in our place. When you say complicated, is that the kind that means "bad idea," or the kind that means you need a second to get there?

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Not bad idea. Just not something I wanted to answer halfway. There are other pieces attached to it.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You make that sound like there's a spreadsheet behind it. I asked because it stopped feeling casual a while ago, at least on my side. If this is a bad time, you can just say you don't see me that way.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: No, that's not it. I've actually been trying to figure out how to tell you I accepted a job out of town, and I didn't want you to think my weirdness was about you. I should've said it sooner.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Out of town. That's... not where I thought this was going. How far and how soon is "accepted"?

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Another city, about three hours away. I start in six weeks, so I'd be moving before then. I kept waiting for a cleaner moment and managed to make it worse instead.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Six weeks is not a tiny detail to tuck behind mustard and frozen peas. But the part before that wasn't nothing, then. You weren't just being polite at home and weird out here.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: No. The timing is terrible, but that's different from what you asked. I didn't want the first real version of this to sound like a packed suitcase.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: It does sound a little like one. Still, you answered fast when I gave you the easy exit. So what were you planning to say before the moving boxes took over the script?

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Probably something less smooth than I'd prefer. That I wasn't looking at those dinners like errands, and that leaving doesn't cancel what started before the offer came through. I don't know what shape that can take yet, but I didn't want silence making the decision for both of us.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: If you're going to stand over the coffee table with that look, just say it. Mom's mug is still there, by the way. Try not to knock it over.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I just want a straight answer about earlier. Did something get changed before I got there? Everybody kept talking like I missed a step no one bothered to mention.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Plans shifted. It happens. You're making this bigger than it was.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then make it smaller for me. Tell me who said what, and when. Because I walked into the living room and somehow I was the last person catching up.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: There isn't some grand timeline to reconstruct. A meeting got canceled, people moved on, and you came in halfway through the cleanup. That's all.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Except that's not all. This note was on the table before I came back in, and it points me one way while everyone else was already acting on something else. Why leave this and then say none of it matters now?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Because it doesn't matter now. The meeting didn't happen, nobody died, and the whole house doesn't need a cross-examination over a folded scrap of paper.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You keep calling it a scrap of paper like that explains why it showed up. I'm not asking for a courtroom speech. I'm asking why the story keeps changing every time I ask one basic question.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: The story isn't changing. You're pulling at wording because you want one neat version that makes the whole afternoon line up. Sometimes people just get wires crossed.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Wires crossed would mean somebody corrected it once they saw the problem. Instead I got this, and then a shrug. You knew more than you're saying.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You want me to confess to being in the house when messages were flying around? Fine, I was here. That still doesn't make this some deliberate operation.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: No, what makes it deliberate is this line right here. 'No point dragging everyone back for nothing'—you say things like that all the time, especially when you're trying to wrap a problem before anyone argues with you. You wrote this before I even asked you about today, didn't you?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Lower your voice. Yes, I wrote it. Mom texted that the meeting was off, and I left the note so nobody would keep circling back and turning it into another production.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You could have said that the first time I asked. Instead you watched me chase some vague mix-up like I was imagining the gap. That's the part that lands badly, not the canceled meeting.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I didn't think this would turn into an audit of my phrasing. I saw Mom's message, I handled it, and then you came in already wound up about being left out. Adding another layer in the middle of that wasn't going to help.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Handling it would have included telling me the same thing everyone else got. You don't get to decide I can be managed with a note and a brush-off. Next time, if you step in, you say so.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Fine. I should've told you I saw the message first and that I put the note there. I was trying to keep the room from turning into one more family pileup, and I picked the wrong shortcut.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Shortcuts like that cost more than the extra minute would have. I'm not going to keep guessing around you. If we're cleaning this up, it starts with no more selective versions.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: The line barely moved and we're already at the light again. I brought the flyer because they sent home another copy, and the school is right there if you want to look at the front page before we pull in. It lays out the lunch groups and the activities.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Keep it folded. We've already talked about this. I need you to let me watch the road.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: I'm not blocking your view. I'm saying they don't treat it like some little extra thing after class. It's in the middle of the day.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: It's not happening. They can build the day around it all they want; that doesn't change the answer.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You keep saying it like this is about paperwork. It isn't. When everybody else goes one way and our kid goes the other, that lands somewhere.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: What lands somewhere is a school deciding it gets to package up what's right and hand it out. That's not their lane. We don't outsource that.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Then call it what you want, but noon still comes every day. Group tables, partner projects, the whole routine keeps moving whether we approve of the packet or not.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: So now this is about routine and fitting in. That's exactly how they get people to swallow things they shouldn't. A glossy handout and a full schedule don't make it harmless.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Do you want them sitting alone because of this? Because that's the part you keep stepping around. Friends matter at that age more than any brochure ever will.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Don't do that. Don't make this into me picking some abstract point over our kid. You wave that paper around like the only thing at stake is whether lunch feels awkward.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Awkward is not what I said. I said it touches lunch, activities, the kids they already know. That's not nothing, no matter how much you flatten it.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I'm not flattening anything. I'm saying some things don't become acceptable just because they make the day easier. If the light would change, maybe we could stop circling the same point.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: We're circling because you won't say why this has to be a wall. Every answer is one sentence, and then that's it. That makes it sound like you're finished before anyone else gets to speak.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: This is not about convenience. I already gave my word we would opt out because I won't let the school define our kid's morals.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You already said that to the other house? I didn't know that. I was told they'd be separated from their friends at lunch if we do that.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Separated how? By who, exactly? If a teacher said that, then I need the actual policy, not just a line on a flyer.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Their teacher mentioned the club kids eat together and get grouped together after. It sounded like the ones outside it get placed wherever there's room. That's why I kept bringing up lunch.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: That should have been the first thing out of your mouth. I heard lunch and activities and thought you were trying to sell me on convenience. If they're using social sorting to force this, that's another problem.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: I wasn't trying to sell the club. I was trying to keep one consequence from turning into three. Maybe before we sign anything else, we ask the school what they do for kids not in it.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Fine. I'll call before pickup and ask for that in writing. The answer on the club stays where it is until somebody explains why opting out means a kid loses their table.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Your tea's gone cold. You haven't touched it since I got here. Sit down for a minute, Taylor.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I'm fine where I am. You can say whatever you came to say without arranging me first.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I'm not arranging you. I'm looking at a box of tissues on the table and you standing by the window like the room's too small. That usually means something.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: It means I like air. And the tissues were already out before you arrived, if that's part of the case you're building.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You dropped off the map for two weeks, then sent three-word replies like legal disclaimers. People notice. I notice.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You're not 'people.' And short replies are still replies. I'm handling it.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Handling it how? Because from out here, it looks a lot like shutting doors and hoping nobody knocks loud enough.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: From out here, you don't get much of a view. This isn't something I need to unpack with you.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You don't have to do this by yourself. Before you cut me off for saying that, listen: I talked to Erin because she was worried too.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Of course you did. You hear one vague thing and suddenly there's a committee.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: There isn't a committee. She said there was a scare, that you've been acting like if you keep everything neat and quiet it won't become real. I came because silence can get dangerous fast.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: What gets dangerous fast is people deciding they know my life because they're uncomfortable with not being told everything. You barging in here with your lowered voice doesn't make this care.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You do not have to pretend you're fine just because you want control. That isn't strength, it's just a different way of disappearing.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I am not pretending. I already know what this is, I saw the doctor, and I chose not to tell you because it is my decision. You don't get to turn privacy into evidence against me.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You saw the doctor. Okay. I didn't know that. I should have asked one more time and stopped there.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Yes, you should have. Every sentence tonight came with your hand already on the steering wheel, and that was the whole problem.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You're right. I made it sound like a verdict when it should have been a question. If you want distance, keep it; if you need something later, I can manage to wait for you to say so.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Waiting would help. And not recruiting people. I'm tired, Shiloh, but that doesn't mean I'm lost.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You just took over half the table again. And the rubric's buried under three library books like that's going to make it less annoying.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: It is annoying, which is why this version helps. Look, if we switch to a shorter source list, the whole draft cleans up fast.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: The rubric is right there. It says annotations for every source, and that doesn't read like a suggestion.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: This is the cleaner way, trust me. We don't need to turn a five-page project into a tax audit.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Trust you based on what, exactly? Because from over here it looks like you're pointing at the screen and trying to skip the part with the work.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I'm trying to skip the pointless part. We already have the sources, the argument, the quotes—dragging out full annotations for all of them is just clutter.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Clutter is still safer than handing in something that gets bounced. If we're putting both our names on it, I'm not crossing my fingers because your draft looks prettier.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: So that's it, then? You circle one line with your pen and we're stuck doing the longest version no matter what?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: No, we're stuck doing the version that matches the sheet unless there's an actual reason not to. I am not ignoring the rubric just because you feel good about it.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Then read this. Professor Alvarez said a condensed source list is fine for this assignment as long as the sources are clearly tied to the argument. What if we use the shorter source list for the final copy but keep brief notes for ourselves so you still feel covered?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You had that the whole time? That would've been useful about five minutes ago. Brief notes work.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Yeah, probably better than me tapping the screen like it was going to magically convince you. You want to handle the private notes if I format the final list?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Fine, but I'm keeping them next to each source so nobody has to dig later. And send me that email after this, because I'm not quoting your memory in a footnote war.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Deal. I'll paste the email into our doc too, and I'll keep the source list lean enough that it doesn't sprawl all over page four.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Look at us, suddenly capable of advanced governance in the silent floor. Scoot the laptop back a little and I'll start with the journal articles.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Yes, bossy stranger at table seven. I'll take the books and trim the list, and then you can tell me if page four still offends your sense of order.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: You done with the bench, or are you taking another set? This treadmill keeps resetting the incline every time I step off.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Take your time. You've been hard to reach lately anyway, so I guess waiting is the theme this week.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I've just been busy. And the two dinners after here got messed up, I know.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Yeah, they did. First it was 'running late,' then it was a one-line text at nine, and then after that it was basically calendar updates.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I wasn't trying to make a whole production out of it. Work's been packed, and by the time I got out, dinner didn't make sense.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Okay, but from over here it didn't exactly read like 'packed.' It read like I got moved to the spare slot after sets and emails.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: That's dramatic. I missed dinner twice, not six months of my life, Jamie.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: See, that's what I mean. I bring up something that changed, and suddenly it's me making up a movie.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I'm saying there is a difference between bad scheduling and some larger story. You started with the dinners, so that's what I answered.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: So what was that supposed to look like from my side? You cancel, send these clipped little texts, come in here, say two words, and keep looking back at the treadmill.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Because I'm trying not to have this in the middle of the weight floor like it's a public hearing. And because every answer I give seems to get treated like evidence.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Then give me something that doesn't sound like you're reading off a receipt. I'm not asking about protein macros.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Fine. I have been off because of my review next week, not because I want distance from you.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I thought you were backing away from me. The way you've been around me lately, that was where my head went.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: No. I should've said something before it turned into missed dinners and robotic texts, because I can hear how that looked.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I can work with 'rough week.' I just can't do the thing where I have to guess whether I still get the after-gym version of you or the email auto-reply.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: That's fair. Next time I'll say it's a bad week before you have to assemble clues from my cancellation messages.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Good. And maybe don't make me compete with a treadmill for eye contact when you're clearing this stuff up.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You didn't have to get me another coffee. The first one's still right there, getting cold. I just needed somewhere that wasn't my apartment.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: You always say that and then steal mine anyway. Here. What happened?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: It's work. I got a message, then a calendar invite for tomorrow, and now my boss isn't answering. Everybody in here is somehow louder than usual.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Okay. What exactly did they say?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: "Need to discuss org changes and your role in them." That's the text. Then a thirty-minute meeting with HR copied on it, which is never there for fun.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Slow down for a second. Was there anything else before that, or just the text and the invite?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: If you're going to tell me I'm reading into this, don't. People don't schedule surprise HR meetings to hand out gold stars.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I wasn't going to say gold stars. I'm asking because sometimes the order matters.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Right, the sequence. Great. First there was a missed call while I was driving, then the text, then the invite, then three hours of nothing.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: A missed call from your boss? And you didn't get a voicemail notification?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I got one. I didn't listen to it. I saw the text first and that was enough. Just say it if you think I'm catastrophizing.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I listened to the voicemail from your boss by accident when it came through my car speakers. You're not being fired; they want you to head the transition team. I should've said that sooner.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You what? Why would you sit there asking me all that first? I have been chewing a napkin for twenty minutes over a project.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Because every time I jump in too fast, you shut the door in my face. And when you pulled your phone back, it looked like you wanted me to stay on your side of the booth and guess.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I thought you were doing that thing where you go all calm and clinical until I sound ridiculous out loud. I didn't want to hand over the phone and get a lecture with foam art. Leading the transition team is still... a lot.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yeah, it's a lot. But it's not a box and a security badge at 9 a.m., and that's a different universe from where you were sitting five minutes ago. Drink the coffee while it's still pretending to help, and then we can figure out what 'a lot' means.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You found the bench. I was about to assume you'd gotten distracted by one of those dogs chasing joggers. The park's doing its late-afternoon postcard thing today.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I noticed. Hard to compete with golden light and athletic strangers. Here, I brought you one.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Oh, wow, look at this. So, is this your very mature post-breakup coffee diplomacy? Sitting all the way over there really sells it.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I can move from the quarantine zone if the bench isn't under legal dispute. And maybe it's just coffee, not a treaty. How've you been?

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Busy enough to become one of those annoying people who says "busy" like it's a personality. Work's been wild. You still doing that thing where you collect three projects and complain about all of them?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Only three would be growth, honestly. The studio's the same, my inbox is still a hate crime, and my neighbor keeps practicing trumpet like he's punishing the block. Some things stay loyal.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Nice, neutral updates. Very safe. You always did know how to make small talk sound expensive.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: You say that like you're not excellent at hiding behind jokes. Also, for the record, this park was your pick, which felt suspiciously curated. Are you still running here, or just pretending to be outdoorsy near the pond?

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I run here sometimes. I sit here more. It's easier to watch people almost crash into strollers than answer texts.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: That does sound like your kind of mindfulness practice. I passed the courts on the way in and half expected to find you humiliating someone at pickup basketball. Kind of disappointing, really.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I retired from public humiliation. Seemed more mature. Speaking of sightings, you looked occupied last week when I saw you downtown.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Downtown narrows it down to half my bad decisions. When was this? And wow, you're doing the casual voice so hard it should get a tax break.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Outside that Thai place on Mercer. You were with someone in a green jacket, laughing like rent had been canceled. I figured either your life got way better or your timing got really interesting.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: That was Nina, my cousin. She was in town for twelve hours and judged my shoes with the intensity of a federal agency. That's the glamorous mystery.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Right. Sure. You can just tell me if the coffees are a guilt offering before you go back to whoever you were with last week.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: There is no whoever; I brought your exact order because I still know it and I wanted this to matter. I sat down there because I couldn't tell if you'd let me get any closer, not because this was some cleanup errand.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: It is my exact order. Even the absurd cinnamon on top. I almost skipped this because of Mercer, so that's... a pretty embarrassing use of my afternoon.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Then maybe we can let Mercer retire from public service. Walk with me after this, and next time I won't pretend the coffee was random. You can even inspect the jacket color in advance.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: If that note is about the electric bill again, don't leave it half done on the table. Cold stuff first, please, and then we can sort the rest. Standing there spinning that mug isn't going to make anything disappear.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: It's not exactly that. I was going to say something when you came in. The groceries can wait a second.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: No, they really can't, and neither can things you start. Lately everything lands in a pile with one sentence written on it, and then I get, 'I was about to.' If there's a problem, say it plainly.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I know how to say things plainly. You're already making it into something else. Just give me a minute.

messages.speaker: Wren
